tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Look down at the shoot tips: pale pointed leaf clusters surround a compact 1–2 cm head of about 1–5 spikelets. The flowering packets sit WITHIN the leafy fascicle, not at the end of a long naked flowering stalk. The true Munroa panels show verified same-taxon habit and flowering, including a locally archived Texas herbarium voucher; none alone proves all minute organs.
tiles.short: Woolly flower packets tucked into sharp leaves
tiles.status: VISIBLE GROSS CUE; SAME-PLANT DETAIL STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · FOLLOW THE ROOTED SHOOT
tiles.details: Trace a rooted perennial crown into short wiry, sometimes radiating stems ending in leaf clusters. Kew describes a dwarf perennial with narrow involute blades about 0.5–1 mm wide, hardened white/cartilaginous margins and sharply pointed tips. The physically archived CC0 Brewster County Texas herbarium sheet provides a preserved rooted specimen reference but does not replace a live same-plant root-to-flower sequence.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENT; CONNECTED LIVE ROOT PHOTO GAP

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS, NOT HEADS
tiles.details: One compact head usually contains 1–5 nearly sessile spikelets. A single mature spikelet is approximately 7–13 mm and typically holds 6–12 fertile florets plus reduced terminal florets. Do not confuse a white tuft, an entire spikelet, and one floret; an attached ripe spikelet with 1-mm ruler is still missing.

tiles.heading: 04 · SEPARATE GLUMES FROM LEMMA
tiles.details: Kew GrassBase: two near-equal persistent 1-veined glumes about 6–8 mm; fertile lemma about 3–5 mm, hairy below, three-veined, and split into two lobes to roughly 40–50% of its length. ONE 1.5–2.5 mm awn arises from the notch between the lobes. These are published values, not verified image measurements; no microscopic arrows are justified.

tiles.heading: 05 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: Expose the INNER blade–sheath junction and distinguish its actual ligule from neighboring sheath-edge hairs. Kew GrassBase reports a 0.5-mm hair fringe; a federal Western Grass Manual reports roughly 0.3–0.5 mm; a Flora of North America derivative reports 3–5 mm. This unresolved source disagreement means no hard ligule-length threshold is safe. Photograph several voucher-confirmed collars face-on at 10–20× with a 1-mm bar.

tiles.heading: 06 · DON'T CONFUSE HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS
tiles.details: Panels 7–8 (1-based) depict Erioneuron pilosum for comparison, NOT Munroa. Erioneuron has woolly clubs elevated on mostly bare upright stalks; Munroa encloses its woolly spikelets among pointed shoot-tip leaves. Under 20× Munroa's lemma has a deep notch and long glumes, whereas E. pilosum has a shallow lemma notch and relatively shorter glumes. Do not treat pale color or a hair-fringe ligule as a species-specific shortcut.
tiles.short: Munroa flowers nested; Erioneuron heads raised
tiles.status: FIELD LOOK-ALIKE CUE; MATCHED DISSECTIONS NEEDED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: FLUFFGRASS — LOOK AT GROUND LEVEL: a tiny perennial with pointed white-edged leaves clustered around woolly flowering packets tucked INTO the leafy shoot tips, rather than on raised bare stalks. Follow a connected stem and inspect one mature spikelet: usually 6–12 florets, two long near-equal glumes and a hairy deeply 2-lobed lemma with ONE short awn from its notch. The ligule is hair-fringed, but published ligule lengths conflict; measure an actual opened collar rather than using an absolute length cutoff. Compare Erioneuron pilosum, whose compact woolly heads are held ABOVE the basal leaves on slender, mostly leafless stalks.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Expose the INNER blade–sheath junction and distinguish its actual ligule from neighboring sheath-edge hairs. Kew GrassBase reports a 0.5-mm hair fringe; a federal Western Grass Manual reports roughly 0.3–0.5 mm; a Flora of North America derivative reports 3–5 mm. This unresolved source disagreement means no hard ligule-length threshold is safe. Photograph several voucher-confirmed collars face-on at 10–20× with a 1-mm bar.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Kew GrassBase: two near-equal persistent 1-veined glumes about 6–8 mm; fertile lemma about 3–5 mm, hairy below, three-veined, and split into two lobes to roughly 40–50% of its length. ONE 1.5–2.5 mm awn arises from the notch between the lobes. These are published values, not verified image measurements; no microscopic arrows are justified.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS / Erioneuron pilosum: low perennial bunch, but SMALL TIGHT PALE CLUB HEADS are carried on LONG, mostly leafless erect stems well ABOVE the short basal leaves. FLUFFGRASS / Munroa pulchella: 1–5 compact woolly spikelets are enclosed WITHIN a whorl/cluster of sharp, sometimes nearly white leaves at the TOP of short stems, often angled down and sometimes rooting at nodes; the leafy flowering fascicle, not just woolly color, is a key distinction. Fluffgrass's two long pointed glumes are about as long as its lower spikelet and its fertile lemma is DEEPLY TWO-LOBED (about half its length) with a single stout awn between lobes. In Erioneuron pilosum the glumes are generally SHORTER than the first floret and the lemma notch is very shallow; both have hairy floral organs and hair-fringe ligules, so neither trait ALONE separates them. Other low tuft grasses and tiny Aristida can look fuzzy in drought; check the enclosed short inflorescence and individual florets under magnification. Older DASYOCHLOA PULCHELLA and ERIONEURON PULCHELLUM refer to this Munroa species, NOT the separate species Erioneuron pilosum.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: ARCHIVED — Patrick Alexander's exact-taxon flowering/habit reference
panels.caption: Original source-identified fluffgrass photograph stored in the project. Inspect the leafy flowering clusters; do not identify the true ligule, separated glumes, deeply bifid lemma or awn from this photograph without pixel verification.
panels.creator: Patrick Alexander from Las Cruces, NM
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: CLOSE DETAIL — pointed enclosing leaves and nested woolly flowering region
panels.caption: Alex Abair's CC BY 4.0 close-up makes the key visible: stiff thin acute-pointed leaves form a starburst and surround woolly flowering clusters near the shoot tips. The arrows identify a genuine pointed LEAF and the pale hairy FLOWERING REGION, not individual awns, glumes, or dissected florets. The apparent fuzz is not proof of a particular lemma organ.
panels.creator: Alex Abair
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

markers.label: Pointed enclosing LEAF — not an awn

panels.label: 2 · ACTUAL FLUFFGRASS — close leafy spikelet clusters against sky
panels.caption: Alex Abair's Commons photo (2018) shows a close-up of pale pointed leafy fascicles and compact flowering tufts held at a stem tip. This is the SAME accepted Munroa taxon under its older name Dasyochloa pulchella. It does NOT show a dissected floret: do not mistake long pointed surrounding LEAVES for lemma awns.
panels.creator: Alex Abair
panels.modifications: Saved RGB JPEG, stripped EXIF/GPS and resized to <=2600px longest side; original composition preserved

panels.label: 3 · ACTUAL FLUFFGRASS — second licensed real-species reference
panels.caption: Jim Morefield's photo depicts western fluffgrass (Dasyochloa/Munroa pulchella) photographed in California. This is a different source photograph from the Don Rideout and Alex Abair images, useful for seeing variation in plant habit and fluffy leafy head arrangement. Rooting, 0.5-mm ligule and dissected lemma are not confirmed from this reference.

memory_rule: FLUFFGRASS = woolly MULTIFLORET heads DOWN IN sharp LEAFY STARS; HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS = woolly compact clubs held UP on mostly bare STALKS. Munroa confirmation: 1–5 heads/spikelets, LONG near-equal glumes, DEEP bifid hairy lemma with ONE short awn between lobes, short hair-fringe ligule.
